title: Is Canada more divided these days? Governor General Louise Arbour isn't worried
summary: Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour shares how she's been settling into her relatively new role, and how Canadians can face an increasingly uncertain world together.

image.caption: Governor General Louise Arbour spoke to Matt Galloway in a special episode of The Current, recorded at the National Arts Centre in Ottawa this week. (Michel Aspirot/CBC)

blocks.text: The Current
Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour shares how she's been settling into her relatively new role, and how Canadians can face an increasingly uncertain world together.
King's representative says Canadians can face down threats at home and abroad
LISTEN | Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour speaks to Matt Galloway:
The Current1:14:24The Ottawa you don't know
Canada may sometimes seem more divided as a country these days, but Governor General Louise Arbour thinks what we’re seeing is just “democracy in action.”

“We have a lot that binds us together. We live in a space that allows us to express our different aspirations, different views [and] to do so in a respectful manner,” Arbour told The Current’s Matt Galloway in an interview this week.
“What is there to be scared about?”

Arbour was formerly a Supreme Court justice and the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights. She was installed as Governor General in June, as the country grappled with U.S. President Donald Trump's trade war and his repeated jibes about making Canada the 51st state.
But when asked about her role in holding the country together in face of those threats, she joked that it wasn't in the job description.
“Whoa, whoa. Hold on a second,” she laughed. “Nobody said I had to hold the whole thing together. That's not what I signed up for.”
Governor General on the threats Canada faces right now
Arbour spoke to Galloway about settling into her relatively new role, and how Canadians can face an increasingly uncertain world together. Here is part of their conversation.

You came into this job in a remarkable time. I mean, you have a country under threat, you have the U.S. president talking about a 51st state. You have a referendum in Alberta and the possibility of a referendum maybe in Quebec, as well. When you take a look at that, how do you see your role in holding this country together?

There are lots of moving parts, right? This is a democracy. So what you describe is democracy in action. I mean, we have a lot that binds us together. We live in a space that allows us to express our different aspirations, different views, to do so in a respectful manner.

I don't think there's anything to be concerned about, particularly if you look both sort of geographically at the rest of the world and historically at the state of the world. What is there to be scared about? We're just talking to each other. We're not killing each other.

For the most part, we still have a respectful discourse in our disagreement, so I think we're in very good shape. I'd be frankly [more worried] if we're silently in agreement. There are places where you have to be silently always in agreement. That's very scary.

It may not have been part of the job description, but there is an element of your role in which you do need to speak with Canadians, coast to coast to coast. And how do you think about that at a time when, yes, we are talking to each other, but sometimes we're talking past each other — or we aren't listening to each other.

It's interesting, because you referred both to: I'm talking to people, and I'm listening to people. So I certainly try as best I can to listen. First of all, I have so much to learn, particularly in the interactions I've had so far with a lot of Indigenous communities.

To me [previously], it was all about Indigenous rights, [as] a series of legal concepts. Now I interact with people. I don't have a lot to say, I have a lot to learn. So I think the listening part is not a bad start.
Public space for national debates must be protected, new GG says

The privilege of this kind of function is that I have access and opportunities to an enormous range of different people. From what I did today, which is receiving letters of credence, the ambassadors presenting themselves to Canada. So I saw nine of them today representing a whole range of different countries. And then again, you know, I travel somewhere, I stop in at Tim Hortons and we have a talk. Or I try to listen, not talk too much.

The country is in this moment right now. There's a conversation, a big conversation about who we are and who we want to be, and it's happening with clearer eyes, I think, than perhaps in the past. How do you see us in this movement?

I think there's different ways of looking at it. I think sometimes we wonder about what we look like, how the world sees us, and then how we feel about ourselves. And I think that there's part of us, sometimes, that are unduly romantic about how the world sees us. You know, certainly in my generation it was the image of you could travel the world with a Canadian flag on your backpack and you'll be welcomed everywhere, the world loved us. I think we're sort of back there, but in a sometimes overly romantic way.

How do we feel about ourselves? Certainly in the recent year or so, I think, we've come together with much more of a sense of cohesion in who we are as a nation or in a kind of patriotic way that we hadn't seen expressed that strongly in the recent past.
What should we do with that?

I think we should look after each other, we should empower each other. We're gonna have impact in the world as a reflection of how strong we are together. So I think that that's our first job, is to look after our immediate communities, our togetherness, and just on the strength of that, we have a lot of opportunities to do a lot of good.
